## Limits

### One-sided criterion for a limit

The two-sided limit exists and equals $L$ exactly when both one-sided limits equal $L$:

$$
\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=L.
$$

[Explanation and examples](../lectures/02-limits.qmd#one-sided-limits)

### Limit laws

::: {.statement}

Suppose $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=M$, where $L,M$ are real numbers. Let $c$ be a real constant and $n$ a positive integer.

#### Constant {#limit-constant}

$$
\lim_{x\to a}c=c.
$$

#### Identity {#limit-identity}

$$
\lim_{x\to a}x=a.
$$

#### Sum and difference {#limit-sum-and-difference}

$$
\lim_{x\to a}(f(x)\pm g(x))=L\pm M.
$$

#### Scalar multiple {#limit-scalar-multiple}

$$
\lim_{x\to a}c f(x)=cL.
$$

#### Product {#limit-product}

$$
\lim_{x\to a}f(x)g(x)=LM.
$$

#### Quotient {#limit-quotient}

$$
\lim_{x\to a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=\frac LM,\qquad M\ne0.
$$

#### Power {#limit-power}

$$
\lim_{x\to a}(f(x))^n=L^n.
$$

#### Root {#limit-root}

$$
\lim_{x\to a}\sqrt[n]{f(x)}=\sqrt[n]{L}.
$$

For even roots, require $L\ge0$ and $f(x)\ge0$ for the nearby inputs. Odd roots allow negative values. The same laws apply to one-sided limits.

:::

[Lecture explanation and examples](../lectures/04-limit-laws.qmd#the-limit-laws)

### Substitution for polynomials and rational functions

Let $f$ be a polynomial or rational function. If $a$ is in the domain of $f$, then

$$
\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a).
$$

[Proof and examples](../lectures/04-limit-laws.qmd#polynomials-and-rational-functions)

### Reciprocal powers near zero

For a positive even integer $n$,

$$
\lim_{x\to a}\frac{1}{(x-a)^n}=\infty.
$$

For a positive odd integer $n$,

$$
\begin{gathered}
\lim_{x\to a^-}\frac{1}{(x-a)^n}=-\infty,
\\[0.4em]
\lim_{x\to a^+}\frac{1}{(x-a)^n}=\infty.
\end{gathered}
$$

[Explanation and examples](../lectures/03-infinite-limits.qmd#infinite-limits-and-vertical-asymptotes)

### Squeeze Theorem

Suppose $\ell(x)\le f(x)\le u(x)$ for all sufficiently nearby $x\ne a$. If

$$
\lim_{x\to a}\ell(x)=\lim_{x\to a}u(x)=L,
$$

then $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$.

[Explanation and examples](../lectures/05-squeeze-theorem.qmd#the-squeeze-theorem)

### Fundamental trigonometric limit

For angles measured in radians,

$$
\lim_{\theta\to0}\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}=1.
$$

[Proof](../lectures/05-squeeze-theorem.qmd#the-fundamental-trigonometric-limit) · [Examples](../lectures/05-squeeze-theorem.qmd#trigonometric-limits)

## Continuity

### Continuity of polynomials and rational functions

Polynomials and rational functions are continuous on their domains.

[Explanation and proof](../lectures/06-continuity.qmd#continuity-at-a-point)

### Operations that preserve continuity

Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous on their domains. Then the following functions are continuous wherever they are defined:

$$
\begin{gathered}
f+g,\qquad f-g,\qquad cf,\qquad fg,\\[0.4em]
\frac fg,\qquad f^n,\qquad\sqrt[n]{f},
\end{gathered}
$$

where $c$ is a constant and $n$ is a positive integer. For a quotient, require $g(x)\ne0$; for an even root, require $f(x)\ge0$.

[Proof](../lectures/06-continuity.qmd#operations-that-preserve-continuity)

### Continuity and composition

Suppose $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=L$ and $F$ is continuous at $L$. If $F(g(x))$ is defined for the nearby inputs under consideration, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{x\to a}F(g(x))
&=F\left(\lim_{x\to a}g(x)\right)=F(L).
\end{aligned}
$$

In particular, if $g$ is continuous at $a$ and $F$ is continuous at $g(a)$, then $F\circ g$ is continuous at $a$.

[Explanation and example](../lectures/06-continuity.qmd#continuity-and-composition)

### Continuity of trigonometric functions

The functions $\sin x$, $\cos x$, and $\tan x$ are continuous on their domains.

[Proof](../lectures/06-continuity.qmd#continuity-of-the-trigonometric-functions)

### Intermediate Value Theorem

Suppose $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$. If $N$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then there is a $c\in[a,b]$ such that

$$
f(c)=N.
$$

[Explanation and examples](../lectures/07-intermediate-value.qmd#the-intermediate-value-theorem)

## Differentiation

### Differentiability implies continuity

Let $a$ be in the domain of $f$. If $f'(a)$ exists, then $f$ is continuous at $a$.

[Proof](../lectures/10-derivative-function.qmd#differentiability-implies-continuity) · [Why the converse is false](../lectures/10-derivative-function.qmd#the-converse-is-false)

### Differentiation rules

::: {.statement}

Suppose $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $x$. Let $c$ be a real constant and $n$ any real number.

#### Constant {#constant-rule}

$$
\frac{d}{dx}(c)=0.
$$

#### Identity {#identity-rule}

$$
\frac{d}{dx}(x)=1.
$$

#### Sum and difference {#sum-and-difference-rules}

$$
\frac{d}{dx}[f(x)\pm g(x)]=f'(x)\pm g'(x).
$$

#### Scalar multiple {#scalar-multiple-rule}

$$
\frac{d}{dx}[cf(x)]=cf'(x).
$$

#### Power {#power-rule}

$$
\frac{d}{dx}(x^n)=nx^{n-1}.
$$

The power rule holds for $x>0$ for every real $n$, and wherever both sides are defined for other inputs. For $n=0$, use the constant rule.

#### Product {#product-rule}

$$
\frac{d}{dx}[f(x)g(x)]=f'(x)g(x)+f(x)g'(x).
$$

#### Quotient {#quotient-rule}

$$
\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\right]=\frac{g(x)f'(x)-f(x)g'(x)}{[g(x)]^2}.
$$

Require $g(x)\ne0$.

:::

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/11-differentiation-rules.qmd#section-3.3-the-rules-we-will-use) · [Sums and powers](../lectures/11-differentiation-rules.qmd#sums-constant-multiples-and-powers) · [Products](../lectures/11-differentiation-rules.qmd#products-one-derivative-at-a-time) · [Quotients](../lectures/11-differentiation-rules.qmd#quotients-and-negative-powers)

### Chain rule

Suppose $g$ is differentiable at $a$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(a)$. Then $F=f\circ g$ is differentiable at $a$, and

$$
F'(a)=f'(g(a))\,g'(a).
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\frac{d}{dx}f(g(x))=\textcolor{#0072B2}{f'(g(x))}\,\textcolor{#B44D00}{g'(x)}.
$$

[Explanation](../lectures/14-chain-rule.qmd#the-chain-rule) · [Examples](../lectures/14-chain-rule.qmd#combining-differentiation-rules)

### Power rule for a function

If $g$ is differentiable, then

$$
\frac{d}{dx}(g(x))^n=\textcolor{#0072B2}{n(g(x))^{n-1}}\,\textcolor{#B44D00}{g'(x)},
$$

wherever the power function is differentiable at $g(x)$.

[Proof and examples](../lectures/14-chain-rule.qmd#powers-of-functions)

### Inverse-function derivative

Suppose $f$ is one-to-one and continuous on an open interval containing $a$, is differentiable at $a$, and $f'(a)\ne0$. If $b=f(a)$, then $f^{-1}$ is differentiable at $b$, and 

$$
(f^{-1})'(b)=\frac{1}{f'(a)}=\frac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(b))}.
$$

[Derivation and examples](../lectures/15-inverse-functions.qmd#the-inverse-function-derivative)

## Special functions

### Trigonometric derivatives

For angles measured in radians, on the domain of each function,

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\displaystyle\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x)=\cos x,
&\displaystyle\frac{d}{dx}(\cos x)=-\sin x,\\[10pt]
\displaystyle\frac{d}{dx}(\tan x)=\sec^2x,
&\displaystyle\frac{d}{dx}(\cot x)=-\csc^2x,\\[10pt]
\displaystyle\frac{d}{dx}(\sec x)=\sec x\tan x,
&\displaystyle\frac{d}{dx}(\csc x)=-\csc x\cot x.
\end{array}
$$

The functions $\tan,\sec$ require $\cos x\ne0$; $\cot,\csc$ require
$\sin x\ne0$. Sine and cosine are defined for every real $x$.

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/13-trigonometric-derivatives.qmd#trigonometric-notation-we-will-use) · [Derivations](../lectures/13-trigonometric-derivatives.qmd#using-quotients-to-explain-the-new-formulas)

### Inverse-trigonometric derivatives

With the usual inverse-trigonometric branches, the following derivatives hold on the indicated open domains. Angles are measured in radians. 

$$
\begin{array}{rcll}
\text{(i)}\quad \dfrac{d}{dx}\sin^{-1}x&=&\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}},& |x|<1,\\[13pt]
\text{(ii)}\quad \dfrac{d}{dx}\cos^{-1}x&=&-\dfrac1{\sqrt{1-x^2}},& |x|<1,\\[13pt]
\text{(iii)}\quad \dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}x&=&\dfrac1{1+x^2},& x\in\mathbb R,\\[13pt]
\text{(iv)}\quad \dfrac{d}{dx}\csc^{-1}x&=&-\dfrac1{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}},& |x|>1,\\[13pt]
\text{(v)}\quad \dfrac{d}{dx}\sec^{-1}x&=&\dfrac1{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}},& |x|>1,\\[13pt]
\text{(vi)}\quad \dfrac{d}{dx}\cot^{-1}x&=&-\dfrac1{1+x^2},& x\in\mathbb R.
\end{array}
$$

Here $\cot^{-1}$ takes values in $(0,\pi)$, $\sec^{-1}$ in $[0,\pi]\setminus\{\pi/2\}$, and $\csc^{-1}$ in $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]\setminus\{0\}$.

[Inverse-sine proof](../lectures/15-inverse-functions.qmd#derivatives-of-inverse-trigonometric-functions) · [Worked example](../lectures/15-inverse-functions.qmd#using-inverse-trigonometric-derivatives)

### Exponential slope and the existence of e

For $a>0$, the function 

$$
F(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{a^h-1}{h}
$$

 is well-defined, continuous, and strictly increasing.

There is a unique number $e\in(1,10)$ such that $F(e)=1$.

[Geometric sketch and existence argument](../lectures/17-exponential-logarithmic.qmd#what-is-e)

### Natural exponential and logarithmic derivatives

$$
\text{(i)}\quad \frac{d}{dx} e^x=e^x\quad(x\in\mathbb R),
\qquad
\text{(ii)}\quad \frac{d}{dx}\ln x=\frac1x\quad(x>0).
$$

[Proofs](../lectures/17-exponential-logarithmic.qmd#the-natural-exponential-and-logarithm) · [Examples](../lectures/17-exponential-logarithmic.qmd#worked-examples)

### Exponential and logarithmic derivatives in other bases

For $a>0$, 

$$
\text{(i)}\quad \frac{d}{dx} a^x=a^x\ln a.
$$

 For $a>0$, $a\ne1$, and $x>0$, 

$$
\text{(ii)}\quad \frac{d}{dx}\log_a x=\frac1{x\ln a}.
$$

[Proofs and examples](../lectures/17-exponential-logarithmic.qmd#other-bases)

### Power rule for real exponents

For any fixed real number $n$ and $x>0$, 

$$
\frac{d}{dx} x^n=nx^{n-1}.
$$

The restriction $x>0$ makes this proof work for every real exponent. The rule also holds at other inputs when the particular power function is differentiable there.

[Proof](../lectures/17-exponential-logarithmic.qmd#the-power-rule-for-real-exponents)

## Precalculus

### Inverse functions and the horizontal line test

A function has an inverse function on its range exactly when it is one-to-one. Graphically, this means that every horizontal line intersects the graph at most once.

[Explanation and example](../lectures/00-functions.qmd#one-to-one-functions-and-domain-restrictions)

### Exponent and logarithm laws

For $a>0$, real $r,s$, and positive $M,N$, with $a\ne1$ for logarithms,

$$
a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad a^{r-s}=\frac{a^r}{a^s},\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs},
$$

 

$$
\log_a(M^r)=r\log_a M,\quad
\log_a(MN)=\log_a M+\log_a N,\quad
\log_a\frac MN=\log_a M-\log_a N.
$$

[Lecture explanation](../lectures/17-exponential-logarithmic.qmd#algebraic-laws)

[Implicit differentiation](../lectures/16-implicit-differentiation.qmd) and [logarithmic differentiation](../lectures/17-exponential-logarithmic.qmd#logarithmic-differentiation) are techniques for applying these rules. Follow the lecture links for the steps and worked examples.
